sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A follow-up to Dion Wiggins' maintenance deficit ratio: the numbers checked, our PHP evidence added, and the business model named.
sections.para: Dion Wiggins measured Germany's spend on its PHP website platform against its investment in PHP: 241 to 1. Checked against primary sources, every cut gives two orders of magnitude. Two days after the fix, 109 of 751 downstream products are fixed and no named compromise exists. Open source's business model pays integrators and hosts, not maintainers and packagers.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven lines: the ratio, it holds, downstream unfixed, no named compromise, assessment in a day, the wrong layer paid, AI.
sections.para: Dion Wiggins' ratio for Germany and PHP is 241 to 1, and every cut of the sources gives two orders of magnitude. Two days on, 109 of 751 inventory rows are fixed. No named organisation reports a php2shell compromise. Agents built an independent assessment in a day. The model pays the wrong layer, and AI made finding cheap and fixing scarce.

sections.label: The piece
sections.line: Dion Wiggins' post and article: a maintenance deficit ratio, the whole sovereignty stack, and a warning seven weeks early.
sections.para: Dion Wiggins divides what a government spends migrating onto open source by what it contributes to maintaining it: 241 to 1 for Germany and PHP. Above 10 to 1, Dion says, there is no sovereignty strategy. Dion walks the stack from LibreOffice to core-js, and cites the PHP Foundation's September warning that dependent institutions have no mechanism to fund maintenance.

sections.label: The numbers, checked
sections.line: The ratio holds at 179 to 263 to 1; a few details differ: contract split, grant years, Finland, UK councils.
sections.para: The €108m contract runs four years, €73.2m of it migration. The Sovereign Tech Agency's page lists €205,000 for PHP in 2023 and 2024. Ratios range from 179 to 263 to 1. The PHP Foundation took $730,534 from 536 donors in 2025, with 11 developers. Finland restricted public traffic; the UK figure is one minister's count. Some figures were not checked.

sections.label: Two days on, from our evidence
sections.line: Two days on: 15% of 751 downstream products fixed, no named compromise, and the catalogue still silent.
sections.para: The patch came fast; distribution did not. The Dutch inventory at 12:50 UTC on 23 October lists 751 products: 109 fixed, 222 vulnerable, 389 under investigation. The compromise map finds no organisation naming php2shell as the way in, and CISA's catalogue still lists neither flaw. The shutdowns were decisions under uncertainty, without a map of each site's reach.

sections.label: An assessment in a day
sections.line: Independent assessment no longer needs the maintainers' time: the PHP story's site was built in a day.
sections.para: Dion notes no government could assess the flaw independently on 21 October. The PHP story's site, built in one day by two people and agents from a public evidence vault, graded 70 claims, read the fix in the code, tracked the inventory and mapped compromise. Understanding an incident has become cheap; fixing the code has not.

sections.label: Why this is a business model failure
sections.line: A business model that pays the integrator, platform and host, and sells nothing a buyer can buy from the maintainer.
sections.para: Integrators win contracts, platform companies sell for billions and hosts bill monthly, all selling something procurement can buy. Maintainers and packagers take donations: a missing product, not a funding gap. AI made the imbalance worse: models turned long-known flaws into exploits within days, so discoverers now have more resources than the maintainers who must decide, fix and package.

sections.label: What would work
sections.line: Three fixes: buy maintenance as a product, pay at the trusted source, and measure the ratio everywhere.
sections.para: Pay specialists to maintain the minimal version customers run, with a scope and a service level procurement can buy, via a maintainer line item; one percent of the German contract exceeds the Foundation's year. Pay at the source for signed, timely builds. Measure the ratio in every sovereignty plan and company, and map each site's reach before the next incident.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Ratios are illustrative, some figures unchecked, rows are not servers, the absence is time-bound, the proposals are mine.
sections.para: Contracts and grants cover different periods and scopes, so ratios are illustrative. Several of Dion's figures were not checked and remain Dion's. The inventory counts products, not servers, and under investigation means unassessed. The compromise map is a time-bounded absence as of 20:50 UTC on 22 October. The three proposals are the author's, not Dion's.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Dion Wiggins' post, article and illustration, the PHP Foundation's sources, the STA, the NCSC inventory, CISA and our site.
